page.title: Lesson Overview
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 2 | Page 1 of 6

Lesson Overview: Clarity, Cohesion, and Conventions

Lesson Focus

Primary: MLA.CW.REV.02.
Supporting: MLA.CW.REV.01 and MLA.CW.COM.03. Revise for reader orientation, meaningful connections, and publication-ready control without flattening voice.

What You Will Learn

  • Diagnose ambiguity as intentional or accidental.
  • Repair unclear reference, chronology, spatial logic, and sentence boundaries.
  • Build cohesion through purposeful repetition, transitions, and information flow.
  • Edit conventions according to intended effect and defend deliberate deviations.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 2 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task: Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.
TermMeaningExample
clarityEase with which the intended meaning can be understood.A clear revision names which character “she” refers to.
cohesionConnections that make the parts of a text function together.Repeated images of frost link the opening, conflict, and ending.
coherenceThe overall logical and meaningful unity of a text.Every scene advances the same central conflict, so the story feels coherent.
antecedentThe noun to which a pronoun refers.In “Mara lifted the box before she opened it,” Mara is the antecedent of she.
chronologyThe sequence of events in time.Dates at each scene break help readers follow the chronology.
transitionA signal showing relationship or movement.“Three weeks earlier” marks a transition into a flashback.
lexical chainRelated words repeated or varied across a passage.Tide, current, harbor, and drift form a lexical chain.
given-new flowSentence movement from known information toward new information.The second sentence begins with the key named in the first, then reveals what it opens.
sentence boundaryThe point where one complete sentence ends and another begins.A period repairs the run-on by marking a sentence boundary.
intentional fragmentAn incomplete sentence used deliberately for effect.“Not this time.” is an intentional fragment that sharpens resolve.
usageConventional ways words and structures are used.The editor checks whether the verb agrees with its subject.
house styleA publication’s consistent editorial rules.The journal’s house style requires numerals for dates.

Vocabulary in Action

Match each clue to the precise term. Choose Check, study any mismatch, and retry. This practice is ungraded.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Which revision most improves both clarity and cohesion?

A. Replace every short sentence with a longer one.

Not the strongest choice. Sentence length alone does not clarify references or connect ideas.

B. Name the unclear antecedent and add a transition that shows when the scene shifts.

Correct. Naming the antecedent improves clarity, while the transition strengthens cohesion by showing the relationship between scenes.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 2 | Page 3 of 6

Lesson: The Four-Pass Editorial Protocol

Pass 1 — Reader Orientation

Track who speaks or acts, where the reader is, when events occur, and what each pronoun refers to. Mark every point where a reader could form the wrong mental picture.

Pass 2 — Cohesion and Coherence

Map cause, contrast, sequence, comparison, and return. Use transitions only where relationships are not otherwise visible. Build lexical chains and place known information before new information when clarity requires it.

Pass 3 — Sentence Control

Check boundaries, coordination, subordination, modifier placement, parallelism, tense, and agreement. Preserve a fragment or unusual syntax only when its effect is identifiable and worth the cost.

Pass 4 — Publication Proof

Read aloud; inspect punctuation, capitalization, spelling, dialogue format, paragraphing, and house style. Compare the final version with the original purpose so correctness does not erase voice.

Pause and Choose: Repair Reader Orientation

Draft: “Maya handed Lena the folder after she finished the interview.” The context does not reveal who finished. Which revision is clearest?

A. “After Lena finished the interview, Maya handed her the folder.”
Stronger choice. Naming Lena at the decision point removes the ambiguous antecedent while preserving the original sequence.
B. “After she finished it, she handed her the folder.”
Weaker choice. More pronouns increase ambiguity. A reader cannot build an accurate mental picture when the actors and referents remain hidden.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Visual Diagnostic

SymptomLikely causeTestRepair
Who is “she”?unclear antecedentreplace pronouns with nounsrename at the decision point
Scene feels jumpymissing causal/temporal linkwrite because/therefore/butadd action or transition

Pause and Choose: Correct Without Erasing Voice

A narrator’s fragment—“No door. No window. Just the hum.”—intentionally creates panic. What should an editor do?

A. Combine every fragment into one conventional sentence because fragments are always errors.
Weaker choice. Mechanical correctness is not the only criterion. The fragments have a clear rhythmic and psychological effect, so automatic correction could flatten the voice.
B. Preserve the fragments if the surrounding passage makes their meaning clear and their urgency supports the purpose.
Stronger choice. The editor identifies the deviation, tests its effect, and keeps it deliberately. Control means knowing when a convention serves the reader and when a purposeful exception serves the piece.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

Learning Routes

Diagram reference arrows; read aloud for boundaries; arrange sentence cards and test information order.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 2 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Three Editorial Repairs

Example 1 — Reference and Spatial Logic

Draft: “Maya told Lena she left it beside her chair. When she returned, it was gone.” The pronouns allow several readings. Revision: “Maya told Lena, ‘I left the portfolio beside your chair.’ When Maya returned, the portfolio was gone.” The change clarifies speaker, owner, object, and return.

Pause and Choose: A or B

Which revision most accurately repairs the pronoun problem?

A. Maya told Lena she left it beside her chair. When Maya came back, it was gone.
Weaker response. Naming Maya only once still leaves “she,” “it,” and “her chair” open to multiple readings.
B. Maya told Lena, “I left the portfolio beside your chair.” When Maya returned, the portfolio was gone.
Stronger response. The revision identifies the speaker, owner, object, location, and returning person while preserving the event.

Retry: Close your first choice and open the other. Compare both explanations before continuing.

Example 2 — Cohesion Without Overexplaining

Draft jumps from an argument to a train platform. Revision adds a causal action: “Because he could not answer her accusation, Devon grabbed the envelope and ran for the last train.” The transition works because character choice—not “later”—connects scenes.

Example 3 — Intentional Fragment

Draft: “The alarm sounded. Loud. Red. Unavoidable.” The fragments create impact but “red” lacks a clear referent. Revision: “The alarm sounded. Loud. The red panel pulsed—unavoidable.” Two fragments remain purposeful; the visual relationship becomes legible.

Edit Log

Record issue → reader risk → revision → preserved effect. This proves that an edit supports meaning instead of merely obeying a rule.

Your Turn Before Independent Work

Pause and try: Revise “Jordan told Alex they should move it before they arrived” so every reference is clear without adding a new event.

Check your thinking — open after you try
Teacher model: One clear version is: “Jordan told Alex, ‘Move the display before the visitors arrive.’” The revision names the speaker, listener, object, action, and arriving group.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 5 | Lesson 2 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Clarity, Cohesion, and Conventions

Purpose

Improve clarity and cohesion while using conventions to support meaning and voice.

Complete each numbered part in your notebook. Use precise evidence from your own work and the source provided.

Source for Your Work

Draft: “Nia reached the platform late. The announcement echoed. Her sister had warned her. The ticket was damp. She made a decision. It changed everything.”

1. Plan Before You Work

DecisionYour Plan
Purpose and intended audienceState each clearly.
Most important craft or communication needName the need and evidence.
Success indicatorDescribe what an effective result will do for a reader.

2. Choose and Explain

Which approach demonstrates stronger decision-making? Record A or B, then explain your choice in 2–3 sentences using a lesson concept.

A. Combine every short sentence into one long sentence so the paragraph flows.
B. Clarify relationships among ideas, vary sentence patterns, and use transitions and punctuation where they guide the reader.

3. Apply the Lesson

Revise the draft into a coherent 180–250 word scene. Establish what Nia wants, connect the details logically, vary sentence structure, and maintain correct conventions without flattening the voice.

4. Revise with Purpose

Annotate three changes: one for clarity, one for cohesion, and one for conventions. Explain the specific problem each change solves.

Before You Submit

  • All four numbered parts are complete.
  • Your work applies the lesson skill to a specific creative product.
  • Your explanation identifies a decision and its effect on readers.
  • Your revision meaningfully improves the work, not only its appearance.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Checkpoint: Clarity, Cohesion, and Conventions

Put the lesson together through analysis, decision-making, writing, and purposeful revision.

Purpose

Show that you can understand the lesson concept, apply it in original work, and explain your decisions. Complete every numbered item and submit your responses with your Checkpoint work.

New Source: The Missing Connection

Jules found the unsigned letter beneath the register. The café was closing. Rain covered the windows. His sister had not called in six months. He turned the sign to CLOSED. The handwriting leaned sharply to the left.

Clarity makes meaning easy to follow. Cohesion connects ideas and details into a unified flow. Conventions are agreed rules of grammar, punctuation, spelling, and usage.

Part 1: Analyze the Source

  1. What relationship among the details is implied but not yet clear? Cite two details that need a stronger connection.
  2. Where would a transition, sentence combination, or reordered detail improve cohesion? Explain the effect.

Use this response pattern: Make a precise claim, cite the relevant detail, and explain how the detail proves the claim.

Part 2: Choose A or B

3. Which sequence produces a clearer, more cohesive revision?

A. Correct spelling and punctuation first; if every sentence is correct, the passage is automatically cohesive.
B. Clarify the relationship among ideas and improve their sequence first, then edit conventions so the final language is accurate.

Record A or B in your submission and explain your choice in 2–3 sentences. The answer is not revealed here because this item is part of your graded written work.

Part 3: Create and Apply

4. Transform the source into a 450–550 word complete scene.

  1. Opening: Establish Jules’s immediate situation and the letter’s significance.
  2. Development: Connect the café, sister, and handwriting through purposeful transitions and a logical sequence.
  3. Turning point: Reveal a decision or discovery.
  4. Resolution: End with a consequence that follows clearly from the choice.

After drafting, complete three passes: (1) clarity of meaning, (2) cohesion and transitions, and (3) conventions. List one change from each pass and explain its purpose.

Plan before drafting: Decide what the audience should understand, how each section will build that understanding, and which details will do the most work.

Part 4: Revise With Purpose

5. Choose one choppy section and revise its sentence boundaries or order. Read it aloud and make one additional change for flow.

Do more than correct spelling. Revise organization, meaning, evidence, or craft so the work becomes clearer and more effective.

Before You Submit

  • Every numbered item is complete.
  • Analysis includes specific evidence and reasoning.
  • The creative work follows the required organization and length.
  • The A/B response is recorded and explained.
  • The revision is visible and its purpose is clear.

Mastery Target

A score of 80% or higher demonstrates mastery. Depth, control, and application matter more than unnecessary length.

TOR Help

If you are unsure how to organize your response, choose evidence, or revise meaningfully, contact your Teacher of Record before submitting.
